newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bank workers dig in heels in hostage-taking.
newsitem.headline: French bank workers dig in heels in hostage-taking.

text.p: Angry employees holding hostage the top executives of the Credit Foncier bank dug in their heels on Sunday in the third day of a standoff with the French government over job security and the eventual fate of the bank.

Several hundred employees occupying the plush Paris headquarters of the property lender since Friday announced they would open the bank for business as usual on Monday morning even as they continued to bar the captive executives from leaving.

However they allowed bank governor Jerome Meysonnier to call a news conference inside the bank, where he refused to criticise the staff holding him hostage and held out hopes for a solution that would get around a government plan to dismantle the institution, one of France's oldest.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis has proposed spinning off Credit Foncier's housing loans and commercial business to another group, co-operatively run Credit Immobilier, which has pledged to take 1,500 staff.
The rest of the bank would be wound down, raising the spectre of job losses among the 3,300 people now on the payroll.
The standoff is also a new test for the government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, running a tight spending policy in the run-up to a single European currency.

The government has repeatedly bowed to union protests, raising the question of whether it can stay the course with its austerity budget. It has said it would take five billion francs ($900 million) to keep Credit Foncier in one piece.
Meysonnier, though named to his post by the government, held out the possibility of a venture with a rescue partner rather than the partial takeover the government has proposed.
Union leaders hailed his statement as a step in the right direction.

They also said he appeared to be acting as a go-between between union leaders and the government, an impression strengthened when Arthuis called him on his portable telephone halfway through his news conference.
Credit Foncier manages billions of bonds in French debt and operates low-cost housing loans on behalf of the state.

The 145-year-old private bank ran into deep trouble last year after posting a 10.8 billion franc ($2.0 billion) 1995 loss. After no buyer turned up then, France's conservative government effectively nationalised the bank and is now working on plans to spin off its main activities and wind the rest down.
The government said it was forced to act to prevent a bank collapse wreaking havoc in financial markets, where Credit Foncier was the second largest issuer of bonds after the state.

But the affair rapidly gained wider importance, highlighting close ties between the state and the banking sector, as staff and shareholders smelled an effort to sink the bank and close an embarrassing saga of losses in which the state was involved.
Even when Credit Foncier was private, its top managers were named by the state because of its sensitive role in housing.
Unions say it was these managers who "overloaded" the 1995 results with massive provisions of 13.6 billion francs ($2.5 billion) for reckless property dealings in the late 1980s.
